1.open: Think of a time you waited a long time for something. What was it, and how did the waiting feel?
questions: Verse 5 says Elkanah "loved her even though the LORD had closed her womb." What does it tell you about Hannah's world that she was loved and still deeply hurting?
Verse 7 says the taunting went on "year after year." Why might the place meant for worship have been the hardest place for Hannah to be? Where do you find it hard to show up when you are hurting?
Elkanah asks, "Am I not better to you than ten sons?" (v. 8). He clearly cares, but what is he missing? How can we comfort someone without brushing aside their pain?

Hannah "poured out my soul before the LORD" (v. 15). What do you make of the fact that she brought her raw grief to God, tears and all? When have you been that honest with God, or found it hard to be?
Eli sees a woman praying and wrongly decides she is drunk (vv. 12-14). When have you been misjudged, or misjudged someone else, in a moment of pain?

After Eli says, "Go in peace," Hannah leaves and "her face was no longer downcast" (vv. 17-18), before her situation has changed. What do you think shifted for her? Is there something you have handed to God and still have not seen change?

Hannah says, "I now dedicate the boy to the LORD" (v. 28). Her promise was costly, and the story does not say how she felt. What do you imagine it was like for her, and what makes a promise like that worth keeping, or not?

Hannah's story ends this chapter with an answered prayer. Many people pray for years and the answer does not come the way they hoped. What would you want to say honestly about that, and what do you still hold onto?
1.life: Set aside ten minutes this week to tell God exactly what is weighing on you, without tidying it up, the way Hannah did. If someone in your life is hurting, ask how they are really doing, and listen without trying to fix it.
1.prayer: Thank God that we can pour out our souls to him, just as Hannah did. Pray for anyone in the group who is waiting, grieving or feeling overlooked, and ask for the courage to be honest with God.
1.tip: Question 8 can be painful for anyone who has prayed for something that never came, including children. Do not rush to explain or tidy it up. Let people say honestly that it is hard, and remind the group that Hannah's peace came after she prayed, not after the answer arrived.

2.open: Who is someone you know who quietly kept showing up and doing the right thing, even when nobody noticed?
questions: Hannah begins, "My heart rejoices in the LORD" (v. 1). She had waited years and carried real shame. What do you think it means that her first words are about God and not about her child?
She says, "There is no one holy like the LORD" and calls him a "Rock" (v. 2). What does it mean to you to call God a Rock? When have you needed something that solid?
Verse 8 says God "raises the poor from the dust and lifts the needy from the ash heap." Where have you seen someone overlooked get lifted up? Where have you seen it not happen?
Verses 12 to 17 say Eli's sons "had no regard for the LORD" and treated people at worship with contempt. Why is it especially harmful when those who lead worship abuse their position?
Eli scolds his sons, but they "would not listen" (vv. 23-25). Why is it so hard to correct people we love, and what might Eli have done differently?
God tells Eli, "You have honored your sons more than Me" (v. 29). What might it look like today to put someone or something we love ahead of God, even a good thing?

Verse 25 says the LORD intended to put Eli's sons to death, and many readers find this hard. Christians have long wrestled with how that fits with their own choices. What questions or discomfort does this bring up for you? It is fine to be honest here.
In verse 30 God says, "I will honor those who honor Me, but those who despise Me will be disdained." How does this sit alongside Hannah's song, and with what you have seen in real life?
2.life: Hannah and Samuel are faithful in quiet ways while others around them misuse their power. This week, choose one small, unseen act of faithfulness, such as a kept promise or a kind word, and offer it to God. Also ask yourself whether there is a hard conversation with someone you love that you have been putting off.
2.prayer: Thank God that he lifts up the humble and overlooked, as Hannah's song celebrates. Ask him to help each of you honor him above everything else, and to give you courage to speak truth gently to people you love.
2.tip: Verse 25 ("the LORD intended to put them to death") and the harsh judgment on Eli's family will trouble some people. Don't rush to explain it away. Say plainly that Christians have wrestled with it for centuries, point to the sons' repeated choices in verses 12 to 17 and 22 to 25, and let people voice their discomfort honestly. Also, Hannah's mention of God's "anointed" (v. 10) is read by some as a direct pointer to Jesus and by others as a hope for Israel's kings later read in light of him. Mention it briefly if it comes up and move on.

3.open: Have you ever been sure someone called your name, or woken you up, and it turned out to be nobody? What happened?
questions: Verse 1 says "the word of the LORD was rare, and visions were scarce." What might it have felt like to live in a time when God seemed quiet? When have you felt something like that?
Three times Samuel hears the LORD and thinks it is Eli (vv. 4-8). Verse 7 says he "did not yet know the LORD." Why might it be easy to miss God's voice, even when you are close to the things of God?
Eli is old, nearly blind, and his own family is failing, yet he is the one who realizes it is the LORD calling (v. 8). What does it say to you that God used Eli to help Samuel, even with Eli's flaws?
Eli tells Samuel to answer, "Speak, LORD, for Your servant is listening" (v. 9). What would it look like for you to say that this week? What makes listening hard for you?
Samuel's first message from God is a hard one about Eli's family (vv. 11-14). Why do you think God gave a young boy such a heavy word? What would you have wanted to do in his place?
Verse 15 says Samuel "was afraid to tell Eli the vision." When have you had to tell someone a truth they did not want to hear? What helped, or what do you wish had been different?

When Samuel tells him everything, Eli answers by saying that this is the LORD and that God should do what is good in his eyes (v. 18). Readers differ on whether that is humble trust or tired resignation. What do you hear in it, and why?

Verse 19 says the LORD was with Samuel and "He let none of Samuel's words fall to the ground." What do you think it means to be someone people can trust to speak truthfully? Where do you see that kind of person around you?
3.life: Set aside five quiet minutes each day this week with no phone. Pray Samuel's words in your own way, "Speak, for Your servant is listening" (v. 10), then simply sit and notice what comes to mind. If you are unsure or doubting, say that honestly to God too.
3.prayer: Thank God that he speaks and that he knows each of us by name. Ask for ears that listen, and for courage and kindness when we have to say something hard.
3.tip: Verses 11 to 14 can feel harsh, and someone may ask why Eli's family is judged so severely. Don't rush to defend or explain it away. Point to what the text says: the sons treated God with contempt and Eli did not stop them. Note that Christians read the chapter's purpose differently, some as a pattern for how God calls ordinary people today and some as a one-time turning point in Israel's leadership, and let the group stay with the question without forcing an answer.

4.open: What is a lucky charm, a favorite object, or a habit that you rely on more than you probably should?
questions: After the first defeat the elders ask, "Why has the LORD brought defeat on us before the Philistines today?" (v. 3). What do you notice about the question they ask, and what do you notice about the answer they jump to?
The elders decide to bring the ark "so that it may go with us to save us" (v. 3). What were they hoping the ark would do for them, and how is that different from turning to God himself?
The Israelites shout so loudly that "the ground shook" (v. 5), and the Philistines are afraid. Why might the shouting have felt so convincing, and why did it not change the outcome?

Eli's sons, Hophni and Phinehas, travel with the ark (v. 4), and chapter 2 told us their wrongdoing would bring ruin. What does it say that the people carried something holy into battle without anyone asking whether their hearts were right?
Eli sat by the road, and "his heart trembled for the ark of God" (v. 13). He collapses at the mention of the ark, not at news of his sons (v. 18). What do you make of his reaction?
Phinehas's wife names her son Ichabod, saying, "The glory has departed from Israel" (v. 22). Have you ever felt that God had gone quiet or left? What was that like, if you are willing to say?
This chapter is hard and ends with no comfort. Why do you think the Bible records stories like this without softening them?

What are the things today that we can treat like the ark, as a guarantee of God's help, such as a church, a tradition, a Bible verse or good behavior? How could we tell if we were trusting the thing more than God?
4.life: This week, pick one thing you tend to lean on as proof that things will be okay, such as a routine, a possession or a reputation. Each time you notice it, pause and tell God plainly that you are trusting him and not it.
4.prayer: Ask God to keep you from treating his gifts as if they were him. Pray for anyone in the group who feels that God is far away right now.
4.tip: Many people will want to explain the chapter away, or will struggle with the suffering of people like Eli's daughter-in-law who seem caught in judgment on others. Do not rush to tidy it up. Say that the text is honest about loss, point back to the main question of what Israel trusted, and let someone who feels God is distant speak without being fixed.

5.open: What is something you have kept around long after it stopped working, like an old gadget, a favorite mug or a lucky shirt?
questions: The Philistines put the ark beside Dagon's statue, most likely as a trophy of war (vv. 1-2). Why do people love to display a win over someone else? Where have you seen that in our own day?
Twice the Ashdodites found Dagon "fallen on his face before the ark of the LORD" (vv. 3, 4). What do you think the writer wants us to notice about the two gods in that room?
After the first fall, the people simply "took Dagon and returned him to his place" (v. 3). Why do we so often set back up what has just failed us instead of rethinking it?
Verse 5 says Dagon's priests still would not step on the threshold "to this day." What habits or traditions do people keep without really knowing why?

The men of Ashdod said, "His hand is heavy upon us" (v. 7). Then they sent the ark away, again and again, rather than turn to God. What does that tell us about the difference between fearing God and wanting to be close to him?

This chapter is hard to read. People die and the survivors suffer, and the writer does not soften it (vv. 11-12). What do you feel when you read that? Say it honestly, even if what you feel is unease or doubt.
Israel lost the battle, yet in this chapter God is never shown as beaten. How might that change the way we think about times when it looks as if God has lost?
What is one thing you tend to trust to keep you safe or secure, other than God? What would it look like to hold it more loosely?
5.life: This week, pick one thing you lean on for security, such as money, a schedule, a reputation or a routine. Each time you notice yourself leaning on it, pause and tell God honestly where you are.
5.prayer: Ask God to show you anything you trust more than him. Pray for the courage to be honest about your doubts, and for anyone in the group who feels that life has gone against them.
5.tip: Verses 6 to 12 describe sickness and death, and some people will struggle with a God who does this. Christians differ on whether to read the fallen statue and the plague as literal events directly caused by God, or as a story shaped mainly to show that Israel's God was not defeated. Say so plainly, let people voice their discomfort without hurrying to fix it, and keep returning to what the chapter clearly shows: God is not beaten, even when his people are.

6.open: Have you ever tried to return something you borrowed or took by mistake, and found it was more awkward than you expected?
questions: The Philistines ask their priests, "What shall we do with the ark of the LORD?" (v. 2). What does it tell you that they turn to their own advisers, and what would it look like for someone today to seek help the same way?
The priests warn, "Why harden your hearts as the Egyptians and Pharaoh hardened theirs?" (v. 6). When have you seen stubbornness keep someone from doing what they knew they should?

The Philistines set up a test to learn whether the plague was God's doing or "happened by chance" (v. 9). When something unexpected happens to you, good or bad, what makes you decide whether it was chance or something more?

The cows went "straight up the road toward Beth-shemesh" and never strayed "to the right or to the left" (v. 12). What do you make of this picture, and what do you think the Philistine rulers were thinking as they followed behind?
The people of Beth-shemesh "were overjoyed at the sight" of the ark (v. 13). Where have you felt that kind of joy at something returning or being restored?

Then God struck down people there "because they looked inside the ark of the LORD" (v. 19). Christians read this differently. How does this verse sit with you, and what questions does it raise that you would be willing to say out loud?
The people ask, "Who can stand in the presence of the LORD, this holy God?" (v. 20). How would you answer that question today, and what does it mean to you that God is both near and holy?
6.life: This week, pay attention to one moment when something unexpected happens, good or bad. Instead of passing over it, stop and ask God honestly what, if anything, he might be saying through it. Be willing to leave the question open.
6.prayer: Thank God that he is holy and also wants to be known. Ask for honesty about the hard parts of the chapter and for a heart that does not harden when God gets our attention.
6.tip: Verse 19 will likely stir up strong reactions, and the number of dead is itself debated, with some manuscripts reading seventy and the standard Hebrew text reading far more. Name the difficulty plainly, say Christians read it differently, and make room for people who are troubled by it without rushing to explain it away.

7.open: What is something you keep on a shelf or in a drawer only because it reminds you of a certain time or person?
questions: Verse 2 says that for twenty years Israel "mournfully sought the LORD." What do you think those long years of waiting were like for ordinary people?

Samuel says, "If you are returning to the LORD with all your hearts, then put away the foreign gods and Ashtoreths among you" (v. 3). Why might real return to God involve letting go of something, and not only feeling sorry?
The Baals and Ashtoreths were gods people trusted for rain, crops and a good life. What do people trust today to give them security or a good life?
At Mizpah the people fasted and confessed, "We have sinned against the LORD" (v. 6). Why might saying that out loud, together, matter? What makes honest confession hard?

When the Philistines marched, the Israelites "feared" and asked Samuel, "Do not stop crying out to the LORD our God for us" (vv. 7-8). What do you do first when you are afraid, and what would it look like to turn to God first?

The text says the LORD answered Samuel, and that he "thundered loudly against the Philistines" (vv. 9-10). Some people find it easy to believe God answers prayer and some find it hard. Where are you today, and what has shaped that?

Samuel set up a stone and said, "Thus far the LORD has helped us" (v. 12). He did not say God had solved everything, only that God had helped so far. Why might that be an honest and helpful way to look back?

If you looked back over a hard stretch of your life, is there a moment you would mark with a stone, and what would you write on it? If nothing comes to mind, what would you want to be able to write someday?
7.life: Choose a small stone, or write on a card, one way God has helped you so far. Keep it where you will see it this week, and tell one person the story behind it.
7.prayer: Thank God for help you have already received, even if it came slowly or looked different than you hoped. Ask him to show you anything you are trusting in his place, and for courage to bring your fears to him first.
7.tip: Verse 3 can sound like God's help depends on Israel cleaning up first, and some members may hear it as pressure or shame. Point out that the people were already mourning and seeking the LORD (v. 2), and that Samuel's call is an invitation to come home. Also be ready for the quiet person who has not seen God answer like this; let them say so without fixing it.

8.open: When you were a kid, what was something everyone else had that you really wanted too?
questions: Samuel's sons "turned aside toward dishonest gain, accepting bribes and perverting justice" (v. 3). Why do you think the elders' complaint was a fair one? What do you do when leaders let you down?
The elders say, "Now appoint a king to judge us like all the other nations" (v. 5). What do you think they were really hoping for? What would you have wanted in their place?
Samuel's demand did not please him, so "he prayed to the LORD" (v. 6). What does it tell you that he took his hurt to God before he answered the people?
God says, "it is not you they have rejected, but they have rejected Me as their king" (v. 7). What do you think it looks like today to want something other than God to rule or rescue us?
God tells Samuel to listen to the people, but also to "solemnly warn them" (v. 9). What does it say about God that he warns them and then lets them choose?
Samuel says the king "will take" again and again (vv. 11-17). Which of these takings would bother you most, and why?
The people refuse to listen to Samuel and insist that they must have a king (v. 19). Have you ever wanted something so badly that you stopped listening to good advice? What happened?
They want to be "like all the other nations" (v. 20). Where do you feel the pull to blend in, and where do you feel unsure whether God is really enough? Answer as honestly as you can.
8.life: Think of one thing you are counting on to make you feel safe, such as money, a leader, a plan or other people's approval. This week, tell God honestly how much weight you are putting on it, and ask him to help you trust him with it.
8.prayer: Thank God that he listens even when we ask for the wrong things. Ask him to show you where you look to something else to rescue you, and pray for leaders you know, that they would serve and not take.
8.tip: Christians read this chapter differently. Some think asking for a king was wrong in itself, others think it was wrong only in its motive and timing, since Deuteronomy 17 already allows for a king. Say that plainly, then keep the group on what the text shows: God warns, the people choose, and God stays with them. Do not let the talk turn into an argument about modern politics.

9.open: What is the longest you have ever spent looking for something you lost, and where did you finally find it?
questions: Verses 1 and 2 tell us about Saul's family, his looks and that he was "a head taller than any of the people" (v. 2). Nothing is said about his character. What do we tend to notice first about people, and why?
The story starts with a dull family errand that drags on for days. Where in your own life do the ordinary, boring parts seem to end up mattering more than you expected?
When Saul wants to give up, his servant says there is "a man of God who is highly respected" nearby (v. 6). Who has pointed you toward help when you were ready to quit?
Verse 16 says God told Samuel, "I have looked upon My people, because their cry has come to Me." What does that tell us about how God sees people in trouble?
If you have ever cried out for help and felt no answer, how would you describe that honestly? There are no wrong answers here, and it is fine to say you are unsure.
Saul answers Samuel with "Am I not a Benjamite from the smallest tribe of Israel" (v. 21). Why do people so often brush off the idea that they matter? When have you done that?

Samuel gives Saul the best seat and a portion of meat, saying "It was set apart for you" (v. 24). What is it like to be welcomed before you have done anything to earn it, and how does that picture God's welcome to us?

Christians differ on whether this story shows Saul's kingship mainly as God's gift to a suffering people or as a concession to people who had rejected God as their king. What in the chapter would you point to for each view?
9.life: This week, take notice of one ordinary errand or interruption and ask God what he might be doing in it. Then tell one person, in a sentence or two, that you see something good in them.
9.prayer: Thank God that he hears the cry of his people and cares about small, ordinary lives. Ask for ears to listen for his word, and for honesty about the doubts and fears each person brings.
9.tip: People may jump ahead to how Saul's reign ends. Gently keep the group in this chapter, where Saul is humble, unsure and surprised. Let the question about unanswered cries stay open without rushing to fix it, and let people simply say what they feel.

10.open: Have you ever been picked for something, a team, a job or a role, and felt sure you weren't ready? What was that like?
questions: Samuel pours oil on Saul's head and asks, "Has not the LORD anointed you ruler over His inheritance?" (v. 1). What do you think it meant to Saul to be told he was chosen, when he had only set out to find lost donkeys?
Samuel gives Saul a string of very specific signs on the road (vv. 2-6). Why might God give signs like these, and when have you wanted a sign of your own?

Verse 9 says "God changed Saul's heart," and verse 6 says he would be "transformed into a different person." What do you think that change looked like on the inside? Where have you seen God change someone, or wondered whether he could change you?
People who knew Saul asked, "Is Saul also among the prophets?" (v. 11). Have you ever surprised people who thought they knew you? How did they react?

When his uncle asks what Samuel said, Saul tells him about the donkeys but not "what Samuel had said about the kingship" (vv. 14-16). The text does not tell us why. What reasons could you imagine, and when have you kept something big to yourself?

Samuel tells the people they have "rejected your God, who saves you from all your troubles and afflictions" (v. 19), yet he also says of Saul, "Do you see the one the LORD has chosen?" (v. 24). Readers differ on whether the king is mainly a gift or a concession. How do you see both things sitting together?

When the lot falls on Saul, he cannot be found, because "he has hidden himself among the baggage" (v. 22). What makes a person shrink back from something others are sure is theirs to do? If you are honest, what is one thing you might be hiding from?
Some men go with Saul, but some "worthless men" doubt him and ask, "How can this man save us?" (v. 27). Saul "remained silent about it." When you are doubted or mocked, what helps you respond well?
10.life: Think of one task or role you have been avoiding because you feel unready. This week, take one small step toward it, and tell one trusted person so they can pray for you.
10.prayer: Thank God that he calls ordinary, hesitant people and is with them. Ask him for honesty about where you are hiding, and for steady hearts in the face of doubt or mockery.
10.tip: Verses 17 to 19 can leave people unsure whether having a king was good or bad. Say plainly that readers see it differently and that the chapter seems to hold both, then steer the group back to Saul's own reactions: his hiding, his silence and his change of heart.

11.open: Think of a time someone showed up for you right when you needed help. What did it mean to you?
questions: Nahash's offer was to put out "everyone's right eye and bring reproach upon all Israel" (v. 2). What does this tell us about the kind of enemy Jabesh was facing, and why would shame matter as much as pain?
The elders asked for seven days to find someone to save them (v. 3). When have you been backed into a corner and had to reach out for help? What was that like?
Saul was "returning from the field, behind his oxen" when he heard the news (v. 5). What do you notice about where we find him, and what might that say about how God works through ordinary people?
When Saul heard, "the Spirit of God rushed upon him, and he burned with great anger" (v. 6). Is there anger that can be good? How can we tell the difference between that and anger that harms?
Saul's summons was harsh, and yet "they came out together as one man" (v. 7). What brings people together in your community, church or family, and what pulls them apart?

After the victory the crowd said, "Bring those men here so we can kill them!" (v. 12). Saul answered, "No one shall be put to death this day, for today the LORD has worked salvation in Israel" (v. 13). Why might mercy be so hard right after a win?
Saul gave the credit to the LORD instead of himself (v. 13). Where do you find it easy or hard to give credit away, and what do you do when you are not sure God had a hand in something?
The people gathered at Gilgal and "rejoiced greatly" (v. 15). When did you last celebrate something together with others, and what made it good?
11.life: This week, think of someone who has wronged or mocked you, or someone you have an edge over. Look for one small way to show them restraint or kindness instead of getting even, and thank God for any good that came your way.
11.prayer: Thank God for the ways he rescues and for the people he uses to help. Ask for the humility to give him credit and the grace to show mercy when we have the upper hand.
11.tip: Verses 7 and 11 describe a violent summons and a slaughter, which can unsettle some people. Don't rush past that. Acknowledge it is hard, note that the chapter is about rescue from a cruel threat, and steer toward Saul's mercy in verse 13. If the Gilgal "renewal" comes up, mention in a line that readers differ on whether it reaffirms Saul's earlier selection or reflects a separate account of how he became king.

12.open: Who is someone you trusted completely when you were growing up, and what made you trust them?
questions: Samuel asks, "Whose ox or donkey have I taken?" (v. 3). Why might he want his record cleared before he steps aside? What does it show about the kind of leader he has been?
In verses 6 to 11 Samuel retells the story of Israel forgetting God, getting into trouble, crying out, and being rescued. Why do you think he goes back over history before talking about the king?

Samuel says the people asked for a king "even though the LORD your God was your king" (v. 12). What was the people really looking for when they asked, and what do we look to for that same kind of security today?
Verse 14 says if both people and king follow the LORD, "all will be well." What does it tell you that the same condition applies to everyone, from the ordinary person to the king?
Some readers think the chapter treats having a king as wrong in itself, and others think the problem was the people's reasons for wanting one. Which way does the chapter read to you, and why?
The thunder at harvest made the people afraid and aware of their wrong (vv. 17 to 19). Have you ever had a moment that made you see something about yourself more clearly? What was that like?

Samuel tells the people not to be afraid, and then tells them not to turn away from the LORD even though they have done wrong (v. 20). Why do you think he urges them to stay close to God right after naming their sin?

Verse 22 says "the LORD will not abandon His people, because He was pleased to make you His own." If you find that hard to believe right now, what makes it hard? If you do believe it, what helps you hold on to it?
12.life: Think of one thing or person you lean on to feel safe, like a leader, a paycheck, a plan or your own strength. This week, tell God honestly about it. Then do one small thing that shows you are trusting him too, such as praying for someone as Samuel did.
12.prayer: Thank God that he does not abandon the people he has made his own. Ask him to show you where you have been trusting something else, and for the courage to turn back to him with your whole heart.
12.tip: Verses 17 to 19 can sound like God is being harsh, and someone may ask why the people were so afraid. Don't rush to defend or explain it away. Point the group to verses 20 to 22, where Samuel answers their fear with comfort and a promise, and let the chapter's ending set the tone.

13.open: When was the last time you had to wait longer than you wanted for something important, and how did you handle it?
questions: Verse 6 says the Israelites hid "in caves and thickets, among the rocks, and in cellars and cisterns." What does fear make people do, and where do you see that in your own life?
Verse 8 says Saul "waited seven days for the time appointed by Samuel." What do you think those seven days felt like for him, and what was happening around him as he waited?
Saul says, "I felt compelled to offer the burnt offering" (v. 12). How does he explain what he did, and how does his explanation sound to you?

Samuel says, "You have acted foolishly," and tells Saul he did not obey the LORD's command (v. 13). Christians differ on what Saul's real wrong was and whether the judgment seems fair. What stands out to you in this scene?
Verse 14 says the LORD has sought "a man after His own heart." What do you think that phrase means, and what would you want it to mean for you?
Saul's army shrinks to about six hundred men, and only he and Jonathan have weapons (vv. 15, 22). Have you ever felt outmatched or under-equipped for what was in front of you? What was that like?
Saul wanted the LORD's favor, but he went about it his own way (v. 12). Where are you tempted to do a good thing in the wrong way, or at the wrong time, because waiting feels unbearable?
If waiting on God feels hard, silent or even pointless right now, what would you honestly say about it? You can pass if you prefer, but this is a safe place to be truthful.
13.life: Pick one thing you are anxious to fix or decide this week. Before you act, stop and pray about it for a few minutes, then ask a trusted friend whether you are acting from wisdom or from impatience.
13.prayer: Ask God for patience when the pressure is rising and the waiting is long. Pray for trust to follow him even when you cannot see what comes next, and thank him that he is faithful when we fail.
13.tip: Many people feel Saul's punishment is harsh for what looks like a small mistake, and that is a fair reaction. Let the group say so, note that Christians read the passage differently, and then steer toward Saul's fear and impatience, which most of us can recognize in ourselves.

14.open: Have you ever taken a leap of faith, big or small, that you weren't sure would work out? What happened?
questions: Jonathan says, "Perhaps the LORD will work on our behalf" (v. 6). Notice he says perhaps, not certainly. What do you make of the way he steps out with hope but no guarantee?
Jonathan says, "Nothing can hinder the LORD from saving, whether by many or by few" (v. 6). Where do you feel outnumbered or too small for the task in front of you?
His armor-bearer answers, "I am with you heart and soul" (v. 7). Who has stood beside you in something hard, and what difference did it make?
Verse 15 says "panic spread from God." The writer credits God for a victory that began with two men climbing a cliff. How do you think human courage and God's work fit together here?
Saul orders that no one eat before evening, and the soldiers end up "faint" (vv. 24, 28). What can happen when a leader's rule sounds devoted but leaves people worn out?
Jonathan says his father "has brought trouble to the land" (v. 29). When have you had to disagree with someone in charge, and how did you handle it?
The soldiers said, "Never! As surely as the LORD lives, not a hair of his head will fall to the ground" (v. 45). What does it look like when ordinary people speak up to protect someone?
God does not answer Saul that day (v. 37). If you have ever felt that God was silent, what was that like, and what do you do with it now?
14.life: Jonathan took one small, concrete step and left the result with God. This week, choose one thing you have been putting off out of fear, take the first small step, and tell one friend so they can stand with you.
14.prayer: Thank God that he can save "by many or by few." Ask for courage to take the next faithful step, and for wisdom and humility for anyone in the group who leads others.
14.tip: Verses 37 to 45 are confusing, and Christians read them differently. Some think Jonathan was truly at fault for breaking an oath he never heard, and others think the story mainly shows how rash Saul's oath was. Say so plainly, don't try to settle it, and steer the group back to what is clear: Jonathan's trust in God, and the cost of Saul's hasty words.

15.open: Tell about a time you were sure you had done a job the right way, and then someone pointed out what you missed.
questions: Samuel reminds Saul that he was "once small in your own eyes" before God made him king (v. 17). How can success or a position change the way a person listens to God?
Saul spared "the best of the sheep and cattle" and destroyed only what was "despised and worthless" (v. 9). Where do people today keep the best for themselves and give God what is left?

When Samuel confronts him, Saul says, "I have carried out the LORD's instructions" (v. 13). Then he blames the troops and says the animals are for sacrifice (vv. 15, 21). Why is it so easy to explain away what we did instead of simply owning it?
Samuel says, "obedience is better than sacrifice" (v. 22). What do you think he means, and what are some religious things we can do that might stand in for listening to God?
Saul finally says, "I feared the people and obeyed their voice" (v. 24). Where have you seen fear of other people's opinions quietly steer a decision, whether yours or someone else's?

Many readers find the order to destroy the Amalekites, children and infants included (v. 3), deeply troubling, and Christians read it differently. Some see it as God's judgment in a unique moment, some as exaggerated ancient war language, and some read it in light of Jesus. What questions or feelings does this passage stir up in you, and what do you do with them?

Saul says "I have sinned" twice (vv. 24, 30), yet he also asks Samuel to "honor me now before the elders." (v. 30). What do you notice about the difference between being sorry and wanting to look good?
The chapter ends with Samuel mourning for Saul and with the LORD regretting that He made Saul king (v. 35). What does it tell you about God that grief and judgment sit side by side here?
15.life: This week, notice one time you are tempted to explain, soften or shift blame instead of simply saying what happened. Try saying it plainly, to God and to one other person if it involves them.
15.prayer: Ask God for ears that listen before hands that act. Ask for honesty about where fear of others has steered you, and for trust that you can bring failure to Him.
15.tip: Verses 2 and 3 will likely stop the conversation, and that is fine. Say plainly that Christians disagree and that being troubled is not a lack of faith. Give it some time, then bring the group back to what Saul does with a clear word from God, so the night does not stall on one verse.

16.open: When you were a kid, were you ever picked last or overlooked for something? What was that like?
questions: God tells Samuel to go and anoint a new king, and Samuel answers, "How can I go?" (v. 2). When has God asked you to do something that felt risky or frightening?
God gives Samuel a plan to go and hold a sacrifice, and says, "I will show you what you are to do" (v. 3). Why might God give direction one step at a time instead of all at once?
Samuel sees Eliab and thinks, "Surely here before the LORD is His anointed" (v. 6). Why do you think Samuel, a prophet, made this mistake so quickly?

God says, "the LORD does not see as man does. For man sees the outward appearance, but the LORD sees the heart" (v. 7). Where do you see people being judged by looks, rank or success today, including in church?

When Samuel asks if these are all the sons, Jesse mentions the youngest, who is out tending the sheep (v. 11). Have you ever felt like the one nobody thought to send for? How does this scene land with you?

After David is anointed, "the Spirit of the LORD rushed upon David from that day forward" (v. 13), yet David goes back to ordinary life and serves in Saul's court. What does this say about how God prepares people?

Saul is tormented, and his servants help by finding someone to play music (vv. 15-18). Christians read the "spirit of distress" in different ways, as a real spirit or as a description of deep despair. However you read it, what can this teach us about caring for someone who is struggling?
If you are honest, do you find it easy or hard to believe that God sees your heart and not just your performance? What makes it hard, and what would help?
16.life: This week, pay attention to the snap judgments you make about people from how they look, sound or what they own. Pick one person you tend to overlook and do one kind, specific thing for them.
16.prayer: Thank God that he sees the heart and not just the surface. Ask him to help you see people the way he does, and to bring comfort to anyone in the group who feels overlooked or weighed down.
16.tip: Verses 14 to 16 about the "spirit of distress" may stir up strong questions or personal stories about mental health. Say plainly that Christians read this differently, don't try to settle it, and keep the focus on caring for people who suffer. Make sure no one feels their own struggles are being labeled.

17.open: What is the biggest thing you ever faced as a kid that seemed huge at the time, and how did it look to you later?
questions: Goliath's armor and spear are described in great detail (vv. 4-7), and then Saul and all Israel were "dismayed and greatly afraid" (v. 11). What kinds of things feel that big and that well armed in your life right now?
For forty days the Philistine kept coming out morning and evening (v. 16). Why might a daily threat wear people down more than a single scary moment?
David asks, "Just who is this uncircumcised Philistine, that he should defy the armies of the living God?" (v. 26). What does David see that the soldiers seem to miss?

His brother Eliab accuses him of "pride and wickedness of heart" (v. 28), and Saul says, "You are just a boy" (v. 33). Have you ever been dismissed or underestimated? How did you respond, and how did it feel?

David points to the lions and bears and says, "The LORD, who delivered me from the claws of the lion and the bear, will deliver me from the hand of this Philistine" (v. 37). How can remembering what God has done before help with a new fear?
Saul's armor did not fit, and David said, "I am not accustomed to them" (v. 39). Where are you tempted to face a problem with someone else's tools instead of what you actually have?
David says, "the battle is the LORD's" (v. 47). What do you make of that? If you find it hard to believe right now, or hard to see in your own life, what would help you say so honestly?

Some readers see this story as a model of trust for anyone facing a giant, while others see it as God's chosen king winning a battle his people could not win. Which way of reading it speaks to you more tonight, and why?
17.life: Name one "giant" you are facing this week. Write down one way God has helped you before, then take one small, simple step toward it using what you already have, not what you think you should have.
17.prayer: Thank God that he is not small and not afraid. Ask for honest trust where you feel outmatched, and pray for anyone in the group who feels overlooked or worn down.
17.tip: The group may rush to name personal "giants" and treat the story as a pep talk. Gently remind them that David's confidence rests on the LORD, not on his own courage, and that some giants in real life do not fall quickly. Leave room for people who feel they are still waiting.

18.open: Think of a time someone close to you got praise or good news you were hoping for. What was your first reaction?
questions: Verse 1 says "the souls of Jonathan and David were knit together." What makes a friendship that deep, and who has been that kind of friend to you?

Jonathan gave David his robe, tunic, sword, bow and belt (v. 4). Many readers see this as Jonathan handing over his own place as heir. What would make it possible to give up something like that for a friend?
The women sang, "Saul has slain his thousands, and David his tens of thousands" (v. 7). Why do you think one line of a song hit Saul so hard?
Saul asked, "What more can he have but the kingdom?" (v. 8). When someone else's success starts to feel like your loss, what do you think is really going on underneath?
Verse 12 says Saul "was afraid of David, because the LORD was with David but had departed from Saul." What do you notice about how fear and jealousy feed each other in Saul?
Saul's plans keep backfiring, and each time David grows more loved (v. 16). Where have you seen someone's scheming or bitterness end up hurting them most?
David answers the king humbly: "I am a poor man and lightly esteemed" (v. 23). How does David's way of handling honor compare with Saul's? Which is closer to where you are today?

The chapter ends with Saul as "David's enemy" (v. 29), and God is hardly mentioned except as being with David. If you feel unsure where God is in a story like this, or in your own life, what would you honestly say?
18.life: This week, notice one moment when you feel a twinge of jealousy. Name it honestly to God, then do one small thing to cheer on the person who got what you wanted, like a message or a kind word.
18.prayer: Thank God that he is with those who trust him, even when others work against them. Ask him to loosen any jealousy in your heart and to make you a faithful friend like Jonathan.
18.tip: Verse 10 says a spirit of distress was "sent from God," which troubles many people, and verse 27 reports a grim war trophy without comment. Don't try to explain everything. Say that the text describes these things plainly, stay with Saul's jealousy and Jonathan's loyalty, and let people say honestly that parts of the chapter are hard.

19.open: Who is someone who has stuck up for you when you needed it, even in a small way?
questions: Verse 1 says Jonathan "delighted greatly in David," and he chose to warn David even though Saul was his own father. What do you think it cost Jonathan to do that?
In verses 4 and 5 Jonathan reminds Saul of what David has done for him and calls killing David sinning against "innocent blood." Why might speaking up gently work when anger would not?
Saul swears an oath in verse 6, and by verse 10 he is throwing a spear. How can someone mean a promise sincerely and still not be changed on the inside?

Verse 9 says "a spirit of distress from the LORD came upon him." Christians understand that phrase in different ways. What questions or discomfort does it stir in you? It is fine to say you are not sure what to think.

Michal warns David, "If you do not run for your life tonight, tomorrow you will be dead!" (v. 11). She saves his life, but she also uses a household idol and tells a story to her father (v. 17). Which parts of her actions do you admire, and which trouble you? Christians differ on how to think about deception used to protect life.
After the escape, David goes straight to Samuel and tells him "all that Saul had done to him" (v. 18). When you are under pressure or afraid, who do you go to, and what do you tell them?

Three groups of messengers and then Saul himself are stopped when "the Spirit of God came upon them" (vv. 20, 23). What does this scene suggest about who is really in charge, the king with the spear or someone else?
19.life: Think of one person who has stood by you in a hard time and send them a note of thanks this week. Then ask yourself if someone near you is being treated unfairly, and take one small step to speak up for them.
19.prayer: Thank God for the people who have protected and encouraged you. Ask for the courage to be that kind of friend, and pray for anyone in the group who feels hunted, worn down or alone.
19.tip: Verse 9 and Michal's deception are the hard spots. Say plainly that Christians read both differently, name the options briefly, and then bring the group back to the bigger picture: God keeps David alive through very imperfect people and through his Spirit. Do not try to settle either question tonight.

20.open: Who is a friend you could call at any hour, and what made that friendship last?
questions: David asks, "What have I done? What is my iniquity?" (v. 1). Have you ever been treated as an enemy when you felt you had done nothing wrong? What was that like?
Jonathan says, "Whatever you desire, I will do for you" (v. 4). What does it cost him to make that promise, given that he is the king's son and Saul's heir?
Jonathan asks David to show his family "loving devotion" even after David's enemies are gone (v. 15). Why would he think about his children's future at a time like this?
The arrow signal in verses 18 to 22 shows how carefully they planned. When have you had to handle a hard situation quietly and carefully, and what did you learn?

In verse 30 Saul's anger is really about losing his throne, and he says Jonathan's kingdom will never be established while David lives (v. 31). What do you think drives people to hurt others when they feel threatened?
When Saul hurls his spear, Jonathan has to face that his own father wants David dead (v. 33). Where have you felt pulled between loyalty to family and doing what is right?
Verse 41 says the friends "wept together." Is it easy or hard for you to let others see you cry or say goodbye? Why?
Jonathan sends David off with, "Go in peace" (v. 42). If you are unsure whether God is near in a hard season, what would peace look like for you, and what makes it hard to find?
20.life: Think of one friend who has stood by you, and one who may need you now. This week, send a message or make a visit that shows loyalty in a practical way.
20.prayer: Thank God for the people who have stood with you in hard times. Ask for the courage to be a faithful friend, even when it costs something.
20.tip: Verses 17 and 41 are read in different ways. Christians commonly see a deep covenant friendship, while some readers see romantic love, and the text leaves room for the debate. Say so in one sentence, then bring the group back to the loyalty, risk and sacrifice that everyone can see in the chapter.

21.open: When did you last have to improvise because you were caught unprepared?
questions: Ahimelech "trembled" when he saw David arrive with no one (v. 1). What do you think he was afraid of, and what does that tell you about how people saw Saul's court?
David says, "The king has given me a mission" (v. 2), and the story simply reports it. Why do you think the writer tells us this without comment? What do you notice about David here?

The priest has only "consecrated bread" to give (v. 4). Why do you think he was willing to bend the usual rule for a hungry man? When have you seen kindness matter more than getting the details right?
Doeg is described as "detained before the LORD" (v. 7), and we are never told why. What do you notice about how the writer slips in a detail that will matter later?

David takes Goliath's sword and says, "There is none like it" (v. 9). What might it mean to him to hold that sword now, as a man on the run? What past victories do you find yourself leaning on when you are afraid?
In Gath David "took these words to heart and was very much afraid" (v. 12). Why might the words of a song have scared him so much? When has something people said about you left you feeling exposed?

David pretends to be mad, and it works (vv. 13-15). Some Christians see his lies and tricks in this chapter as a lapse in trusting God that leads to harm. Others see them as understandable survival moves the story does not condemn. How do you read it, and what is hard about that question for you?
This chapter shows David scared, hungry and improvising. If you are honest, where does your own trust in God feel thin right now, and what do you do in those moments?
21.life: This week, notice one moment when fear tempts you to bend the truth or hide something. Instead of judging yourself, tell God plainly what you were afraid of and ask for help trusting him in it.
21.prayer: Thank God that he stays with people who are frightened and make poor choices. Ask for honesty about your own fears, and pray for anyone you know who is on the run in some way, whether from trouble, pressure or shame.
21.tip: People will want to rule quickly on whether David was right to lie. Say up front that Christians read this differently, and that the text reports his words without praising or condemning them. Then steer the group toward what fear does to us, and let the question stay open.

22.open: Think of a time you were new somewhere and someone made room for you. What did they do that helped?
questions: David hides in a cave, and "all who were distressed or indebted or discontented rallied around him" (v. 2). Why do you think people in that condition gathered around David? Where do people like that gather today?
David asks for his father and mother to be kept safe "until I learn what God will do for me" (v. 3). What do you do when you are waiting and do not yet know what God is doing?
Saul tells his men, "Not one of you has shown concern for me" (v. 8). What do you notice about how he sees the people around him, and what might be driving that?
Ahimelech answers honestly and says he "knew nothing of this whole affair" (v. 15). He is innocent and still dies. What do you make of a story where the right answer does not save him?

Saul's guards "would not lift a hand to strike the priests of the LORD" (v. 17), but Doeg did it himself (v. 18). What helps a person say no when someone with power gives a wrong order? Where might we face a smaller version of that?

The chapter tells the killing of Nob without comment, and God is not mentioned acting in it. How do you read a passage like this when it is hard to find anything good in it? It is fine to say it troubles you.

David says, "I myself am responsible for the lives of everyone in your father's house" (v. 22). What do you notice about how he treats Abiathar? What would it look like for us to offer that kind of safety to someone?
Abiathar arrives with nothing but terrible news and finds a place to stay: "You will be safe with me" (v. 23). Who has been a safe place for you, or who might need you to be one?
22.life: Think of one person who seems to be on the edge: new, lonely, in debt, or hurting. This week, reach out to them with a message, a meal or an invitation, and simply make room for them.
22.prayer: Ask God to be near the innocent who suffer and to give you courage to refuse what is wrong. Pray for a person you know who needs a safe place right now.
22.tip: This chapter is graphic and leaves many people asking where God was. Do not rush to explain it or tidy it up. Let the group say it is hard, point out that the text itself tells it as a horror, and then turn to David's welcome of Abiathar as a small sign of mercy.

23.open: Who is someone who has stood by you when it would have been easier to walk away?
questions: David asks God, "Should I go and attack these Philistines?" (v. 2), and when his men are afraid he asks again (v. 4). Why might David ask twice, and when do you find yourself wanting a second confirmation?
His men say, "we are afraid here in Judah" (v. 3). How does fear make us less willing to help others? When has fear talked you out of something good?
Saul says, "God has delivered him into my hand" (v. 7), but he is really chasing his own plan. How can we tell the difference between God leading us and our own wants dressed up in God's name?
David learns the town he just rescued would hand him over (vv. 11 and 12). Has someone ever repaid your kindness with a letdown? What did you do with that hurt?

The chapter says, "Day after day Saul searched for him, but God would not deliver David into his hand" (v. 14). David is still on the run, so where do you see God's care in this chapter? If God feels quiet when you are running, what is that like for you?
Jonathan "strengthened his hand in God" (v. 16) and told David he would be king, with Jonathan himself as "second-in-command" (v. 17). What might that cost Jonathan, and why would he do it?

Saul is almost on top of David when news of a Philistine raid pulls him away (v. 27). Some readers see God's hand in the timing, and others see a lucky break. How do you read the timing of rescue in your own story?
23.life: Think of one person who seems worn down or on the run in some way. This week, send them a message or visit, and tell them honestly why you are glad they are in your life, as Jonathan did for David.
23.prayer: Thank God for the people who have strengthened you when you were afraid. Ask for courage to do the same for someone else, and for trust when you cannot see the way out.
23.tip: Verses 11 and 12 can raise hard questions, like why God would warn David instead of stopping the betrayal. Don't try to solve it. Point out that the warning gave David a way out, and let people say honestly what the chapter stirs up in them.

24.open: Think of a time someone treated you unfairly. What did you most want to do in that moment, and what did you actually do?
questions: Saul takes "three thousand chosen men" to hunt one man (v. 2). What does that tell you about Saul at this point in his life?

David's men say this is the day God has delivered his enemy into his hand (v. 4). Why might a good opportunity feel like a sign from God? How can we tell the difference between an opening and a green light?
Afterward "David's conscience was stricken" even though he only cut a corner of the robe (v. 5). When has your conscience bothered you over something small? What did you do about it?
David says, "The LORD forbid that I should do such a thing to my master, the LORD's anointed" (v. 6). What do you think was holding David back: fear, principle, trust in God, or something else?
David says, "May the LORD judge between you and me" (v. 12), and then leaves the matter there. What makes it so hard to leave justice in God's hands when you have been wronged?

Saul weeps and says, "You are more righteous than I" (v. 17). Yet David still goes back to his stronghold (v. 22). What do you make of that? How do we show mercy without pretending trust is fully restored?

Christians read this story differently. Some see a call to respect even unjust rulers, and others see a special case tied to Israel's God-chosen king. How do you think it applies, if at all, to how we treat difficult bosses, leaders or authorities today?
If you are honest, is there someone you find it hard to want good for? You can answer in general terms, or simply say that you are not sure you want to let this go yet.
24.life: Think of one person who has wronged you. This week, pray for them by name once a day, and ask God to show you whether there is one small step toward mercy, or one boundary you need to keep wisely.
24.prayer: Thank God that he is a fair judge who sees what has been done to us. Ask for the trust to leave justice with him, and for help to show mercy where it is hard.
24.tip: Questions 6 and 8 may bring up real pain, and some people may hear mercy as a call to stay in an unsafe situation. Make clear that David spared Saul but did not move in with him (v. 22), so forgiving someone and keeping safe distance can go together. Do not push anyone to share more than they want to.

25.open: What is one small thing that reliably makes you lose your patience?
questions: Nabal is described as "harsh and evil in his dealings" (v. 3), and he sneers, "Who is David?" (v. 10). What do you think lies behind a man like that, who has plenty and still refuses to share?
A servant says David's men were "a wall around us, both day and night" (v. 16). How does it feel when you have helped someone and they act as if you did nothing?
David orders, "Strap on your swords!" (v. 13), and soon says, "In vain I have protected all that belonged to this man" (v. 21). How do you see a hurt turning into rage in these few verses?
Abigail moves quickly, brings a large gift and says, "may the blame be on me alone" (v. 24). What stands out to you about how she approaches an angry man with 400 armed followers?
Abigail reminds David of what God has promised him and of the guilt he would carry for needless bloodshed. What helps you hear a hard word when you are angry and feel you are in the right?
David says, "you kept me from bloodshed" (v. 33), and he thanks both God and Abigail. Who has stopped you from doing something you would have regretted, and how did you respond?
Verse 38 says "the LORD struck Nabal dead." How does that sit with you? Say honestly what it stirs up, whether that is discomfort, questions or something else.
Some readers see this story as God protecting his chosen king. Others also see a darker side of David, who demands payment and swears a violent oath. What do you notice in David, good and bad?
25.life: This week, when you feel the urge to get even or fire off a sharp reply, wait one day before you act. In that time, talk it over with God and with one trusted person who will tell you the truth.
25.prayer: Thank God for the people who have stepped in and slowed you down. Ask for a heart that can hear correction, and for the courage to be that voice for someone else.
25.tip: Verse 38 will raise the question of whether God strikes people down, and the text does not explain how Nabal died. Don't try to settle it. Name the discomfort plainly, let people say what they think, and bring the group back to Abigail and David's turning point in verse 33.

26.open: Have you ever had the chance to get back at someone, even in a small way, and chose not to? What stopped you?
questions: Saul goes out with "three thousand chosen men" to hunt one man (v. 2). What does that tell you about where Saul's heart is, and why might someone keep pursuing a person they once admitted was in the right?
Abishai says, "Today God has delivered your enemy into your hand" (v. 8). Why does a chance like this feel like a sign from God? How can we tell the difference between an open door and a temptation?
David answers, "Do not destroy him, for who can extend a hand against the LORD's anointed and be guiltless?" (v. 9). What does this show you about how David sees both Saul and God?

David says, "the LORD Himself will strike him down" (v. 10). What is hard about leaving justice in God's hands instead of taking care of it yourself? Is there a situation where you are finding that hard right now?
David takes the spear and water jug as proof, then shouts from a safe distance (vv. 12, 13). What do you notice about how he handles this? Why might he keep a distance even after showing mercy?

Saul says, "I have sinned," and promises, "I will never harm you again" (v. 21), yet David hands back the spear and goes his own way (vv. 22, 25). What do you make of that? What might it teach us about forgiving someone and trusting them?
Some Christians read David's refusal as a lesson about never resisting leaders, while others see it as tied to Saul being a king God had specially chosen. How do you hear this passage, and why?
If you are honest, where are you today with God: sure He sees what has been done to you, unsure, or a bit angry about it? What would you want to say to Him about that?
26.life: Think of one person who has hurt you. This week, pray for them by name once a day, and do not look for a way to get even. If you need to keep your distance from them for now, that is allowed. Tell God plainly how you feel.
26.prayer: Ask God for the strength to leave justice to Him, and to show mercy where it costs something. Pray for anyone in the group who is carrying a wound from someone else.
26.tip: Someone may hear this chapter as a call to stay close to a person who is hurting them. Say clearly that David shows mercy but also keeps his distance, and that forgiving is not the same as going back into danger. If someone shares something serious, talk with them privately afterwards.

27.open: When you are worn out and out of ideas, what do you tend to do: push harder, run away, or ask for help?
questions: David says to himself, "One of these days now I will be swept away by the hand of Saul" (v. 1). What had he been through that could lead him to think this? When have you felt that kind of weariness?

David decides "There is nothing better for me than to escape to the land of the Philistines" (v. 1). The chapter doesn't say he asked God first. Why might it be easy to skip praying when we are scared?

David takes his men and their families to live under Achish, the king of Gath (vv. 2, 3). What does it cost to run to a safe place that is also the wrong place? Where do people go today when they are desperate?

David asks for a town of his own and receives Ziklag (vv. 5, 6). Why might a small distance from the king have seemed wise to him? What are some ways we try to keep a little distance from the people who hold power over us?

David raids other peoples and tells the king something else. Verse 11 says he took no one alive so that no one would report, "This is what David did." What does it look like when one decision, made out of fear, leads to the next?

The writer tells us what David did and what Achish thought (v. 12) but offers no verdict. Christians read that silence differently. Some see approval of the raids against Israel's enemies, others see a low point told without comment. How do you read it, and why?
Achish concludes that David "will be my servant forever" (v. 12). He trusts a man who is deceiving him. Where have you seen trust built on a false picture, and what does that do to a person?
If you feel somewhat like David here, tired, cornered and not sure God is paying attention, what would you honestly want to say to God tonight? You can answer in your own words, or pass.
27.life: This week, notice one decision you make out of fear or tiredness. Before you act, stop and tell God plainly what you are afraid of, then ask for his help to choose well.
27.prayer: Thank God that he does not give up on people who are worn down and make poor choices. Ask him to meet each person in the group where they feel cornered, and to give honesty and courage in place of hiding.
27.tip: The raids in verses 8 to 11 can pull the group into a debate about war and violence in the Old Testament. Say plainly that Christians read this differently, then bring people back to what the chapter shows about David: fear, secrecy and lies. Keep the grace in view, since God's story with David does not end here.

28.open: When you are worried about something big the next day, what do you usually do the night before?
questions: Verse 5 says that when Saul saw the Philistine army, "he was afraid and trembled violently." What kinds of things make you feel that kind of fear, and what do you tend to reach for first?
Verse 6 says "the LORD did not answer him by dreams or Urim or prophets." What was Saul asking for, and what might God's silence have meant for him at that point in his story?

In verse 3 Saul had removed the mediums from the land, yet in verse 7 he says, "Find me a woman who is a medium." Why do you think people sometimes turn to the very things they once condemned when they are afraid?
Saul disguises himself and goes at night (v. 8). What does the secrecy tell you about how he felt about what he was doing?

In verse 16 Samuel asks Saul why he is consulting him when the LORD has turned away from him and become his enemy. Christians read this scene differently: some believe Samuel truly appeared, others think a spirit impersonated him, others that the woman staged it. How do you think the group can hold that question loosely while still hearing the chapter's message?
Samuel says Saul's fall came because he "did not obey the LORD" (v. 18). Saul's trouble goes back to choices made long before this night. How do old choices shape the fear we carry now?

After the terrible news, the woman tells Saul, "let me set a morsel of bread before you" (v. 22) and then prepares a whole meal. What do you make of her kindness toward the man who had put her at risk?
Some of us have prayed and felt only silence, as Saul did. If you are willing, how have you handled times when God seemed quiet? It is fine to say you are still in the middle of it.
28.life: This week, when worry rises, notice what you reach for first: your phone, a distraction, a plan, a person. Name it honestly, and then say a short, plain prayer before you do anything else, even if all you can say is that you are afraid.
28.prayer: Ask God to meet anyone in the group who feels afraid or unheard right now. Thank him that we can come to him in the open, not in disguise, and ask for the courage to do that.
28.tip: The medium and the appearance of Samuel will pull the group into debate about the supernatural. Say once, fairly, that Christians disagree about what happened, then steer back to Saul: his fear, his silence from God, and the woman's kindness. Also be gentle with anyone who has known grief or silence from God, since this chapter can touch real wounds.

29.open: Have you ever been told you couldn't come along to something, and later been glad you didn't go?
questions: The Philistine commanders ask, "What about these Hebrews?" (v. 3). Why do you think they were so uneasy about David being in their army?
David had been living among Israel's enemies, and now he is marching with them toward a battle against his own people. What does that tell us about the corner he had backed himself into?

The commanders fear David could win back his master's favor "with the heads of our men" (v. 4). What does this show about how they saw him, and how people can be misjudged by their past or their reputation?
Achish says, "I have found no fault in you" (v. 6), yet he still sends David away. Have you ever been trusted by one person and doubted by others? How did that feel?
David asks, "But what have I done?" (v. 8). Many readers think he was putting on a show of loyalty, and some think he was sincerely upset. How do you read his reply, and what makes you lean that way?

Christians differ on how to judge David's time among the Philistines. Some see a lapse of trust that God rescued him from, and others see shrewd survival with no clear right choice. Which view helps you more, and why?

The chapter never says God stepped in, and yet David is spared from an impossible choice. Where have you seen help arrive in your own life without anyone naming it as God? If you aren't sure God was in it, what do you make of it?
29.life: Think of a hard situation where you felt stuck between two bad options. This week, tell God honestly how it feels, and ask a trusted friend to help you see a way through.
29.prayer: Thank God for the times he has quietly kept you from places you were not ready to go. Ask him for wisdom and honesty in any tight spot you are in right now.
29.tip: People may want to judge David harshly or defend him quickly. Say up front that Christians read his choices differently and that the chapter itself does not tell us what he intended. Keep the group on what the text shows and on their own experience of being stuck.

30.open: When you have had a really bad day, what is the first thing you do to start feeling better?
questions: David and his men "wept until they had no strength left to weep" (v. 4). What does it tell you that the Bible shows grief this raw and doesn't hurry past it?
The men talked of stoning David, even though he was grieving too (v. 6). When life falls apart, how do people around you tend to react, and how do you tend to react?
"But David found strength in the LORD his God" (v. 6). What do you think that looked like in the middle of that mess? What would it look like for you, or what makes it hard to picture?
Before he moves, David asks God, "Should I pursue these raiders?" (v. 8). When a crisis hits, how do you usually decide what to do? What would asking God first change?
Two hundred men were "too exhausted to cross the brook" (v. 10). Where do you feel worn out right now, and how do you honestly feel about being someone who has to stay behind?

The key to the rescue is an Egyptian slave whom his master abandoned, and David's men gave him "water to drink and food to eat" (v. 11). What does this small act of kindness show you? Who might be overlooked around us?

Some of the fighters said the men who stayed behind should get nothing but their families (v. 22). David answered that this was what "the LORD has given us" (v. 23) and that all would "share alike" (v. 24). Why is that hard to accept, and how does it speak to how we think about earning and deserving?
Verses 17 to 20 describe a violent battle, and the text simply reports it. If you are unsure how to feel about that, or about God's part in it, what questions would you want to ask?
30.life: Think of someone who has been left behind lately, worn out, sidelined or overlooked. This week, give them something real: a meal, a call, a few hours of help, or a plain word that they matter, with no strings attached.
30.prayer: Ask God to be your strength in whatever feels burned down or taken right now. Pray for anyone in the group who is exhausted and needs to be carried for a while.
30.tip: Verses 17 to 20 may raise uncomfortable questions about the killing. Don't rush to defend or dismiss it. Say that the text reports it plainly, allow honest questions, and then bring the group back to what the chapter stresses: God's care, the rescue, and the equal shares.

31.open: Who is someone from your past that you still remember kindly, even though you lost touch?
questions: Verses 1 and 2 describe a total defeat. The army flees and Saul's sons, including Jonathan, are killed. What stands out to you about how plainly the writer tells it?
In verse 4 Saul fears the enemy will "torture me," and he asks his armor-bearer to kill him. What do you notice about the state Saul is in at this moment?

The text says Saul "fell on it" (v. 4) and then the armor-bearer did the same (v. 5), and it does not comment on either. Why might the writer simply report it? How can we talk about this part with care, knowing it may touch some people personally?
After the defeat, the people "abandoned their cities and ran away" (v. 7). What does this show about how much depended on one king and one battle?

The Philistines hung Saul's body "on the wall of Beth-shan" (v. 10) and gave credit for the win to their idols. What does this chapter show about how people treat the fallen, and how do we see that today?
The men of Jabesh-gilead "journeyed all night" to bring the bodies home (v. 12). Why do you think they took such a risk for a king who had ended so badly?

Christians read this chapter differently. Some see God's judgment on a disobedient king, and others see a sad story told with sympathy for a broken man. Which of those comes closer to what you notice, and what questions does it leave you with?
If you are honest, where does this chapter leave you: sad, unsettled, or something else? What would you want to ask God about it?
31.life: Think of someone who once helped you, whose life has been hard or who is now forgotten. This week, reach out with a call, a note, or a small act of kindness, and do not wait until it is convenient.
31.prayer: Ask God to be near anyone in the group who is carrying despair or grief. Thank him for the people who have shown loyalty and kindness to you, and ask for the courage to show it to others.
31.tip: Saul's suicide may come up, and someone in the room may have lost a loved one this way or struggled with dark thoughts themselves. Keep the tone calm and gentle, avoid arguing about Saul's final standing before God, and say plainly that Christians disagree on how to read the chapter. Afterwards, check in privately with anyone who seemed affected, and encourage them to reach out to a pastor, counselor, or crisis line if they need support.
